Sporttrade Gets CFTC Approval to Run Its Own Prediction Market Exchange

Published November 4, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Sporttrade, a company that once held state sportsbook licenses in five states, announced this week that it has secured registrations from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to operate as a Designated Contract Market and a Derivatives Clearing Organization. In practice, that means the company is no longer positioning itself as a sportsbook at all — it's building out the exchange and clearing infrastructure that powers a federally regulated prediction market, the same regulatory lane already occupied by Kalshi and other sports-event-contract platforms.

From state-licensed sportsbook to federal exchange

Sporttrade launched in 2022 as one of the earlier entrants in peer-to-peer sports contract trading, eventually operating in New Jersey, Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, and Virginia under state sports betting licenses. It exited all five of those markets in June 2026, shortly after applying to move into the CFTC-regulated prediction market space, and its consumer-facing platform has sat dormant since then while it pursued federal registration.

That registration has now come through. With both a Designated Contract Market registration and a Derivatives Clearing Organization registration in hand, Sporttrade says it will roll out exchange and clearing capabilities in phases, starting with a smaller group of flow and liquidity providers before expanding further. The company is currently taking waitlist signups rather than offering public trading yet.

A broker, not just another app

The more notable shift is Sporttrade's new role in the ecosystem: rather than competing directly for bettors' attention the way it did as a sportsbook, it's positioning itself as back-end infrastructure that other brokers plug into. The company says it's lining up broker partners who would route their own customers' trades through the Sporttrade exchange, and it has named social sportsbook Fliff as one of them — Fliff's integration is contingent on Fliff securing its own regulatory approval to operate as a broker on the exchange.

That positions Sporttrade as a plumbing layer in a prediction-market field that already includes Kalshi, Polymarket, FanDuel Predicts, and DraftKings Predictions, several of which have added sports contracts resembling moneylines, spreads, and totals over the past couple of seasons. Sporttrade is betting that running both the exchange and the clearing side gives it more control over execution quality and pricing than a broker relying on someone else's infrastructure would have.

Why it matters to US bettors

For now, this doesn't change where or how most bettors place a sports wager — Sporttrade has no live consumer product today, and its own build-out is explicitly phased and broker-first rather than aimed at retail users directly. The bigger signal is structural: a company that once needed a state-by-state sports betting license is instead building toward a single federal registration that, if the prediction-market model keeps expanding, could let a wider set of apps offer sports-event contracts without going through traditional state gaming regulators at all. That's the same regulatory tension already playing out in states pushing back against Kalshi and other exchanges, and it's worth watching for anyone trying to understand how sports-contract trading and traditional sports betting might coexist going forward.
